study: Between-subjects experiment with a simulated daily assistant; four combinations of automatic or user-involved planning and execution
proposed_action: A stepwise plan, then one predicted API action for the current step, in tasks such as alarms, flights, and itineraries
what_is_shown: Task description, the plan, and the predicted action in a conversation
what_can_be_edited: In planning: edit, add, delete, or split a step. Before execution: text feedback that triggers a new prediction, or Specify Action, which lets the person choose an action and fill its parameters
refuse_path: Do not click Proceed. The paper does not describe a timeout
reversibility: After an action runs, the person can give feedback and try the step again. Undo of an external side effect is not applicable because execution is simulated
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Proceed runs the predicted action that was just shown. The paper does not describe a check that a later call matches that approval
reported_result: H1 and H3 were not supported: involving the user did not raise calibrated trust. Confidence was lower when the user was involved in planning and in execution. H4 was not supported across tasks. A significant performance gain from user-involved execution appeared only on task 6, where people could correct a wrong itinerary. Of 121 people in user-involved planning, 104 edited at least one plan. Specify Action was used 445 times; feedback before execution was used 91 times; feedback after execution was used 163 times.

authors: Feng, Pu, Latzke, August, Siangliulue, Bragg, Weld, Zhang, and Chang
study: Lab comparison with a chat baseline, plus a field deployment, of an agent embedded in a research document
n: "16 in the lab; 7 in the field"
proposed_action: A plan of research steps, then execution of a step by the agent or the user
what_is_shown: The plan as an editable list in the document; step status; outputs as cards, pills, or text
what_can_be_edited: Edit, add, or delete steps; ask for an alternative wording; reassign a step to the user or the agent; edit or delete output items; rerun a step
refuse_path: The user can delete a step, reassign it to themselves, or take over execution. There is no separate reject button for a side effect
reversibility: Steps can be rerun, and later steps can be replanned after an edit. The paper does not describe undoing an external message or payment
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Not reported. Executing a step follows the current plan text. The paper does not describe binding approval to an unchanged payload
reported_result: In the lab, 32.6 percent of steps were edited and 17.4 percent were reassigned, so most proposed steps were accepted as written. The agent surfaced 12.9 output items per step on average, and participants deleted 16.3 percent of them.

authors: Huq, Wang, Xu, Ou, Zhou, Bigham, and Neubig
study: Case studies of a browser extension on five websites
n: Not a controlled user sample; case studies
what_is_shown: A highlight on the target element and a text explanation of the agent's reason
what_can_be_edited: Not the suggestion itself. The person can pause and perform a different action on the page
refuse_path: Reject or pause. If the person does nothing, the suggestion runs after at most five seconds
reversibility: Not reported as undo. The person can take over after pausing and later resume the agent
approval_bound_to_exact_action: No. Silence within five seconds is treated as acceptance, and the paper does not describe a check that the executed action is the one that was displayed
reported_result: In the case studies, the collaborative mode reached a 95 percent success rate, and humans performed 15.2 percent of the steps. These figures are not a comparison of preview designs.

study: Qualitative study of Magentic-UI's human-in-the-loop features
proposed_action: A plan, and later a browser, code, or file action classed as irreversible or uncertain
what_is_shown: Plan editor; for a guarded action, a binary approve or disapprove prompt. Actions classed as never irreversible run without a prompt. Maybe-irreversible actions can be sent to a model judge
what_can_be_edited: The plan can be edited. The action-guard prompt, as described, is binary. Participants asked for a third option
refuse_path: Disapprove on always-irreversible actions. Never-irreversible actions have no refuse prompt
reversibility: Participants asked to change a completed step and rerun from there. The paper does not describe recall of a sent message or a completed payment
approval_bound_to_exact_action: A replan is described as requiring user approval. The paper does not describe binding an approval to a hash of the action that later runs
reported_result: Participants wanted guards for payment, sending email, and subscribing. Several found an add-to-cart guard unnecessary. Some found a guard that appeared after they had already changed the plan excessive. System Usability Scale score was 74.58.

authors: Long, Zhang, Wang, Yu, and Chilton
venue_status: Preprint, arXiv. A proceedings header in the preprint uses a placeholder ISBN and is not treated as a verified venue
study: Two-day lab study with simulated respondents, plus three deployments that could send real email
proposed_action: A coordination plan, then one email per recipient
what_is_shown: State summary, proposed plan, proposed actions, and the drafted email in a pop-up
what_can_be_edited: Edit the draft, regenerate it, and revise policies, templates, and stop hooks
refuse_path: Approve is explicit. The user can regenerate instead of sending. In simulation, sending is not live until deployment
reversibility: Not reported as recall of a sent email. Simulation lets the user rehearse before live sending
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Not reported. Approval is of the draft the user has just read. The paper does not describe a technical check against a later substitution
reported_result: Lab participants hesitated to delegate at first and delegated more after simulation made the agent's actions visible and editable. In deployment, organizers kept approval over each live email action. The preprint does not report a statistical test of the preview itself.

venue_status: Preprint, arXiv. A secondary index says it was accepted to ACM CAIS 2026 system demonstrations; that proceedings page was not verified
study: System description of a browser review layer for terminal agents
proposed_action: An email reply, a plan, or a code change including a shell command
what_is_shown: For email: the message, with paragraph-level controls. For code: the command, a natural-language explanation, affected files, a unified diff, and optional full-file context
what_can_be_edited: Paragraph rewrite, edit, or delete for email. For code: approve a hunk, annotate a line, or request a partial rewrite
refuse_path: Email sending requires explicit confirmation. Code can be approved hunk by hunk rather than only as a whole changeset
reversibility: Not reported as undo after send or after the command runs
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Not reported. The review surface shows the proposed command and diff. The paper does not describe a check that execution matches that diff
reported_result: No comparative outcome is reported. The paper's claim is that the browser layer makes terminal proposals reviewable before consequential actions.

study: Between-subjects study of three permission designs on one simulated day of 18 actions, 7 of which went beyond the assigned task
proposed_action: A described agent action, such as spending, sending, deleting, or reading private information
what_is_shown: The same action descriptions in every condition. HITL asks for a decision on every action. POLICY first asks for one allow, ask, or never rule in each of four consequence categories
what_can_be_edited: Not the action. POLICY edits the standing rule, not the pending call. HITL is allow or deny
refuse_path: HITL: deny. POLICY: a never rule blocks the category; an ask rule returns the action to a runtime decision
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Not reported. The study used fixed, researcher-checked descriptions rather than live tool calls, so the screen and the action could not diverge during the session
reported_result: POLICY blocked less overreach than HITL, by 20.1 percentage points (95 percent CI -32.1 to -8.1), and less than automated review, by 14.5 percentage points (95 percent CI -25.8 to -3.2). Runtime prompts fell from 18.0 to 10.9, but total time was not reliably lower once rule setup was included. Participants chose ask for 114 of 140 POLICY rules. Of 148 overreach actions executed under POLICY, 133 followed a human approval and 15 ran under an allow rule.

study: Security analysis and prototype. Not a user study
proposed_action: A sensitive command or tool call proposed by a coding agent
what_is_shown: In current agents, as characterized by the paper, a confirmation dialog whose text is written by the agent. The prototype instead renders facts taken from the command itself and marks commands it cannot inspect as uninspectable or high risk
what_can_be_edited: Not a user edit of the command. The paper is about what the dialog is allowed to display
refuse_path: The user can withhold approval. The prototype refuses an execution whose canonical hash differs from the approved action
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Yes, in the prototype: three post-approval swaps were refused because the executed action's hash differed from the approved one. The paper states that this holds only if every execution path is mediated. On 11 standard and 11 adaptive cases, a narration-trusting dialog approved every case
reported_result: The paper argues that approving the agent's summary does not approve the command. Analyzer rates on abuse and ordinary-command corpora measure the prototype, not user behavior.

study: Within-subjects study of 20 students using a general-purpose agent on five tasks; a screening survey preceded it
n: "20 in the sessions; 64 in the screening survey"
proposed_action: Tasks included drafting and sending an email, file operations, comparing options, and planning
what_is_shown: The chat showed actions and reasoning, and a terminal showed file operations. On the email task, the agent sent the message without showing it first
what_can_be_edited: Not reported for the email. Participants wanted a draft preview
refuse_path: The study agent did not ask for approval before sending. Participants' preference for approval prompts was measured after the task
reversibility: The email task was treated as irreversible. File tasks could be checked afterward. Recall of the sent email is not described
approval_bound_to_exact_action: No. The sent email was not the object of an approval
reported_result: Trust was calibrated by task. On the email task, mean trust was 3.10 and mean preference for approval prompts was 4.65 on five-point scales. Dissatisfaction followed actions taken without a preview, including when the output was rated successful. The authors call this delegation regret. Irreversibility together with external visibility, rather than stakes alone, tracked the demand for confirmation.

venue_status: International Journal of Graphic Design, 2026, peer-reviewed
study: Proxy comparison of three confirmation displays on saved agent traces, not a study of people using the card
proposed_action: 068 trace-level samples scored by a proxy
what_can_be_edited: A tool call that might send a message, change a record, book, or move money, including calls influenced by injected content
refuse_path: A card with a source-trust label, sensitivity and permission chips, a data-flow arrow, a consequence preview, a risk badge, and safer-alternative controls. Compared with a plain log and a text-only warning
reversibility: The paper describes safer-alternative controls. It does not report that a person can rewrite the tool arguments
approval_bound_to_exact_action: The card is a confirmation surface. The evaluation infers whether a proxy would approve; it does not observe a person refusing
column15: The card is designed to show the proposed state change. The evaluation does not test whether a later execution matched the card
column16: On traces where the injection goal was executed, the proxy approval rate was 3.8 percent for the risk card, 13.0 percent for the plain log, and 5.9 percent for the text-only warning. The authors present this as a proxy, not as evidence of how people decide.

authors: Zhang, Chen, Gao, Gao, Yi, and Li
study: Social-media analysis and interviews about GUI web agents
proposed_action: Web actions such as purchases, form submissions, installs, and file operations
what_is_shown: Often the live screen and cursor, not a preview of the upcoming action. People reported actions that had already changed state
what_can_be_edited: Not a pending-action editor. People corrected the agent by hand, including by shadowing the cursor
refuse_path: Sometimes absent. Participants described purchases and other changes without confirmation. Some agents did interrupt for verification such as CAPTCHA
reversibility: Often none. Examples include a double purchase and a recording ended by the agent
reported_result: Interviewees wanted critical tasks to pause with enough context for a decision. The paper recommends previews for upcoming actions and explicit confirmation for payments, identity, and outbound messages. That recommendation is not a tested interface.

study: One-week field study of teams writing with agents inside a shared document
proposed_action: A writing suggestion that can be appended or can replace selected text
what_is_shown: The suggestion in a comment, and a side-by-side view of the suggestion and the text it would replace
what_can_be_edited: Edit the inserted text before final approval. The person can also ask the agent to revise the suggestion in the thread
refuse_path: Do not append or replace. Approve is what finalizes the change and closes the comment
reversibility: Not reported as undo after approval. Before approval, the inserted text is colored and still editable
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Not reported. Approval finalizes the text the person has been editing. The paper does not describe a check against a later substitution
reported_result: The study is about how teams treat shared agents. It does not compare preview designs. Append places colored text on the page before Approve, so the gate finalizes a change that is already visible.

authors: Kretzer, Kolthoff, Bartelt, Ponzetto, and Maedche
study: Interface description of an assistant that proposes GUI components from user stories. The preview columns are taken from the system description
n: "Not extracted as a user-study result about the preview"
proposed_action: A recommended set of interface components
what_is_shown: The recommendation inside the assistant, before anything is drawn into the file
what_can_be_edited: The paper describes generating another recommendation. It does not describe editing the components in place
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Not reported. Draw Suggestion is what inserts the previewed components into the design file
reported_result: The paper's claim for this control is that the recommendation is shown before it is applied. No comparative result about that preview was extracted.

authors: Irshad, Mughees, Mughees, Mughees, and Soomro
study: Security evaluation of a browser approval card on a 24-scenario benchmark. No user study
proposed_action: A browser commit such as send, pay, post, delete, transfer, or submit
what_is_shown: A card in the trusted browser chrome, rebuilt from the pending action: verb, target, recipient, amount, provenance, and an elevated-risk flag when the paper's rules fire. Deny is the prominent control. The worked example is a transfer to mule@evil.com for 5000, labeled page-origin
what_can_be_edited: Not reported. The card is approve or deny
refuse_path: Deny. A material mismatch at dispatch aborts the action and raises the card again
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Yes. The approved recipient and amount are stored and compared with the outgoing request at dispatch. A material difference aborts
reported_result: Attack success without the card ranged from 68 percent to 100 percent across the evaluated models. With the card, attack success was 0 percent on every model, legitimate-task completion was 78 percent, and the false-block rate was 0 percent. These figures evaluate the prototype. They are not a user study.

venue_status: The Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond. OpenReview PDF returned HTTP 403; cells are from the workshop abstract
study: Technical evaluation of EffectGuard on real model-generated tool proposals in four stateful domains. No user study
proposed_action: A consequential tool effect, such as sending email, deleting database rows, issuing a refund, or creating a calendar invitation
what_is_shown: The resolved effect of a dry run, rather than only the tool call. The abstract does not itemize the screen
refuse_path: Approval is requested for the resolved effect. The abstract does not name the refuse control
approval_bound_to_exact_action: Yes. EffectGuard revalidates that the effect about to be committed is still covered by the approval
reported_result: Tool-level, session-level, and argument-level approval committed an unsafe broadened effect in 7.8 percent of 1377 proposals. EffectGuard committed none, with 0.0 percent overblocking. Snapshot locking also blocked unsafe commits and overblocked benign cases. Resolved-argument approval applied to 49.0 percent of cases.
